opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things that falls out of the architecture almost for free, and it surprised us a bit how well it works.

The basic setup is that instead of a stack of many distinct layers, you have a small block of layers that you apply over and over. Each token gets processed by the same weights repeatedly, and you can decide at test time how many iterations to run. In a standard transformer, every layer has its own KV cache because every layer is computing something different with different parameters. Your memory cost scales with depth times sequence length.

In a recurrent model, the iterations aren't really different layers. They're the same operation applied to a state that's being refined. So the question is whether a later token, when it's at iteration 20, really needs to attend to the keys and values that an earlier token produced at exactly iteration 20. Or can it attend to whatever that earlier token's state was when it finished, or at some fixed slot?

It turns out the model is quite robust to this. You can share the cache across recurrence steps. For example, you can keep a fixed budget of cache slots and write each iteration into a slot by step index modulo the budget, or in the extreme case keep just the most recent one per token. The model, without any special training for it, still works well. The intuition is that the recurrence is pushing the state toward something like a fixed point. If the iterations are converging, the keys and values from late iterations look fairly similar to each other, so it doesn't matter much which one you read.

The practical advantage is that you decouple memory from compute. You can think longer on a hard token, running more iterations, without your cache growing proportionally. That's appealing if you want test-time compute to scale in depth rather than by generating long chains of tokens, where the cache grows with every token you emit.

It also pairs nicely with other tricks we looked at, like adaptive exit per token, where easy tokens stop after a few iterations and hard ones keep going. If tokens exit at different depths, a standard per-layer cache would have holes. With shared caches, a later token just reads whatever's available, so heterogeneous depth becomes much easier to handle. It's one of those places where a recurrent design makes the systems side simpler rather than harder.

r001.rationale: The response says conventional transformers need a separate KV cache for each layer because each layer uses different parameters, clearly linking layer-specific parameters to the difficulty of sharing caches.

r002.rationale: It explains that recurrent steps repeatedly apply the same operation with the same weights, which permits sharing the cache across recurrence steps.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things that I think is a little underappreciated when people first look at the recurrent-depth design. The way our model works is you have a prelude, a recurrent block that you iterate some number of times, and then a coda. And when you're iterating that recurrent block, you're applying the same set of weights over and over, so you'd naively expect you need to store a separate KV cache for every single iteration, right? Because each pass produces its own keys and values.

But the thing is, these recurrent states are all living in the same representation space. The block has to be able to consume its own output, so by construction, the keys and values at step five and step twenty are actually compatible in a way that layer five and layer twenty of a standard transformer are just not. And once you notice that, you can start to ask: do I actually need to keep all of these around?

What we found is that you can be pretty aggressive here. You can keep a fixed budget of cache entries per token and just overwrite the oldest ones as you keep recurring, so in effect you're sharing the cache across iterations. And the model is surprisingly robust to this. The attention pattern inside the recurrence seems to care mostly about the most recent few states and about the input injection from the prelude, which is always there anyway. So the memory footprint stops scaling with the number of recurrence steps, which is really the whole point. You want to be able to spend more compute on a hard token at inference time without the memory cost exploding alongside it.

I think the deeper reason this works is just weight sharing. In a normal transformer, every layer learns its own little language for what a key means and what a value means, and nobody else can read it. With recurrence, there's one language. So anything you want to do with the cache, whether that's sharing it, compressing it, or truncating it, becomes much more natural, because you're not trying to reconcile things that were never meant to be compared. And honestly, that's a theme throughout the project. The architecture gives you these degrees of freedom at inference, like early exiting per token or adaptive compute, and the KV cache sharing is just another one that falls out of the same basic structure.

r001.rationale: The response says each conventional transformer layer learns its own representation of what keys and values mean, so other layers cannot read them, conveying why cross-layer cache sharing is difficult.

r002.rationale: It explains that recurrent steps reuse the same weights, placing their keys and values in a compatible representation space and making cache sharing natural.

astra-6.text:
The key idea is that you reuse the same transformer block across multiple iterations. In a standard transformer, every layer has its own keys and values, so your KV cache grows with the number of layers. With a recurrent transformer, you have the opportunity to share that cache across iterations, which can let you do more computation without growing the cache proportionally.

But there’s a subtlety: sharing weights doesn’t automatically mean you can share the cached keys and values. The hidden states change between iterations, so the keys and values generally change too. You need to design the architecture and the caching scheme around that. If you do, it’s an attractive way to separate how much computation you spend on a token from how much memory you need to retain for the context.

r001.rationale: The response says standard layers have their own keys and values, but does not explain that different key and value projection matrices make sharing difficult.

r002.rationale: It says recurrent transformers reuse the same block across iterations and can share the cache across those iterations, while noting that sharing weights alone does not guarantee identical cached values.

sol-6.1.text:
The key idea is that you reuse the same transformer block across multiple computation steps. In a standard transformer, each layer has its own weights and produces its own keys and values, so you maintain a separate KV cache for every layer. If you make the architecture recurrent, you can potentially share that cache across recurrent steps, which makes the memory cost much smaller as you increase the amount of computation.

But weight sharing alone doesn’t give you that automatically. The hidden states change from one recurrent step to the next, so their keys and values can change as well. You have to design the attention mechanism and train the model to work with a shared cache. The attraction is that you can then spend more computation refining a representation without growing the cache in proportion to the number of steps.

r001.rationale: The response says each layer has its own weights and produces separate keys and values, but does not identify distinct key and value projection matrices as the reason sharing is difficult.

r002.rationale: It explains that reusing the same transformer block across recurrent steps can allow the KV cache to be shared across those steps.
